Main.sentence: Harvard University is a ___E:private U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_university)___ ___E:Ivy League U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivy_League)___ ___E:research university U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university)___ in ___E:Cambridge, Massachusetts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts)___ , United States.

Founded in 1636 as New College , and later named for its first benefactor, the ___E:Puritan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Puritans_in_North_America)___ clergyman ___E:John Harvard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harvard_(clergyman))___ , it is the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States.
Its influence, wealth, and rankings have made it one of the most prestigious universities in the world.

Harvard was founded and authorized by the ___E:Massachusetts General Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_General_Court#Massachusetts_Bay_Colony)___ , the governing legislature of ___E:colonial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonial_history_of_the_United_States)___ -era ___E:Massachusetts Bay Colony U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony)___ .

While never formally affiliated with any ___E:Protestant denomination U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestant_church)___ , Harvard trained ___E:Congregational U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregationalism_in_the_United_States)___ clergy until its curriculum and student body were gradually secularized in the 18th century.
By the 19th century, Harvard had emerged as the most prominent academic and cultural institution among the ___E:Boston elite U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Brahmin)___ .

Following the ___E:American Civil War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War)___ , under ___E:Harvard president U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Harvard_University)___ ___E:Charles William Eliot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_William_Eliot)___ 's long tenure from 1869 to 1909, Harvard developed multiple professional schools, which transformed it into a modern research university.

In 1900, Harvard co-founded the ___E:Association of American Universities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities)___ .  ___E:James B. Conant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_B._Conant)___ led the university through the ___E:Great Depression U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression)___ and World War II, and liberalized admissions after the war.
The university has ten academic faculties and a faculty attached to ___E:Harvard Radcliffe Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Radcliffe_Institute)___ .

The ___E:Faculty of Arts and Sciences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Faculty_of_Arts_and_Sciences)___ offers study in a wide range of undergraduate and graduate ___E:academic disciplines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_discipline)___ , and other faculties offer graduate degrees, including professional degrees.

Harvard has three campuses:  the main campus, a 209-acre (85 ha) in Cambridge centered on ___E:Harvard Yard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Yard)___ ; an adjoining campus immediately across ___E:Charles River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_River)___ in the ___E:Allston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allston)___ neighborhood of ___E:Boston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)___ ; and the medical campus in Boston's ___E:Longwood Medical Area U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Longwood_Medical_and_Academic_Area)___ .  ___E:Harvard's endowment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University_endowment)___ , valued at $53.2 billion , makes it the ___E:wealthiest academic institution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_colleges_and_universities_in_the_United_States_by_endowment)___ in the world.   ___E:Harvard Library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Library)___ , with more than 20 million volumes, is the world's largest ___E:academic library U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_library)___ .

Harvard alumni, faculty, and researchers include ___E:188 living billionaires U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_by_number_of_billionaire_alumni)___ , ___E:8 U.S. presidents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_United_States_by_education)___ , ___E:24 heads of state and 31 heads of government U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Harvard_University_politicians)___ , founders of notable companies, ___E:Nobel laureates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Nobel_laureates_by_university_affiliation)___ , ___E:Fields Medalists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fields_Medal)___ , ___E:members of Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ , ___E:MacArthur Fellows U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Fellows_Program)___ , ___E:Rhodes Scholars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhodes_Scholarship)___ , ___E:Marshall Scholars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marshall_Scholarship)___ , ___E:Turing Award Recipients U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing_Award)___ , ___E:Pulitzer Prize U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize)___ recipients, and ___E:Fulbright Scholars U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulbright_Program)___ ; by most metrics, Harvard University ranks among the top universities in the world in each of these categories. [Notes 1] Harvard students and alumni have also collectively won 10 ___E:Academy Awards U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards)___ and ___E:110 Olympic medals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_American_universities_with_Olympic_medalist_students_and_alumni)___ , including 46 gold medals.

Harvard was founded in 1636 by a vote of the ___E:Great and General Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_General_Court)___ of the ___E:Massachusetts Bay Colony U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony)___ .

Its first headmaster, ___E:Nathaniel Eaton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Eaton)___ , took office the following year. In 1638, the university acquired ___E:English North America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_North_America)___ 's first known ___E:printing press U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press)___ .

The same year, on his deathbed, ___E:John Harvard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Harvard_(clergyman))___ , a ___E:Puritan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puritans)___ clergyman who had emigrated to the colony from England, bequeathed the emerging college £780 and his library of some 320 volumes;  the following year, it was named ___E:Harvard College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_College)___ .

In 1643, a Harvard publication defined the college's purpose: "[to] advance learning and perpetuate it to posterity, dreading to leave an illiterate ministry to the churches when our present ministers shall lie in the dust."

In its early years, the college trained many Puritan ___E:Congregational U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Established_Congregational_churches)___ ministers  and offered a ___E:classical curriculum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_education)___ based on the English university model exemplified by the ___E:University of Cambridge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cambridge)___ , where many colonial Massachusetts leaders had studied prior to emigrating to the colony.

Harvard College never formally affiliated with any particular ___E:Protestant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism)___ denomination, but its curriculum conformed to the tenets of Puritanism.
In 1650, the charter for ___E:Harvard Corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_and_Fellows_of_Harvard_College)___ , the college's governing body, was granted.

From 1681 to 1701, ___E:Increase Mather U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Increase_Mather)___ , a Puritan clergyman, served as Harvard's sixth ___E:president U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Harvard_University)___ .
In 1708, ___E:John Leverett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Leverett_the_Younger)___ became Harvard's seventh president and the first president who was not also a clergyman.

Harvard faculty and students largely supported the ___E:Patriot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution))___ cause during the ___E:American Revolution U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Revolution)___ .

The earliest known official seal of Harvard University, commonly referred to as the Seal of 1650 or the In Christi Gloriam seal, features a square shield bearing three open books arranged around a central chevron.
This design symbolizes the pursuit of learning under divine guidance.

The motto IN CHRISTI GLORIAM ("To the glory of Christ") appears prominently on the seal, which is encircled by the Latin inscription SIGILL COL HARVARD CANTAB NOV ANGL 1650, meaning "Seal of Harvard College, Cambridge, New England, 1650." This seal reflects the original religious mission of the institution.

In 1885, the Harvard Corporation adopted a revised design known as the Appleton Seal, based on an earlier version created by President Josiah Quincy in 1843. Designed by William Sumner Appleton (Harvard AB 1860), the seal features a triangular shield bearing three open books with the motto VERITAS ("Truth").

Surrounding the shield is the motto CHRISTO ET ECCLESIÆ ("For Christ and the Church"), and the outer border bears the inscription SIGILLVM ACADEMIÆ HARVARDINÆ IN NOV. ANG. ("Seal of Harvard College in New England").
This version of the seal sought to harmonize the university's intellectual pursuits with its ecclesiastical roots.

In the 19th century, Harvard was influenced by ___E:Enlightenment Age U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Enlightenment)___ ideas, including reason and free will, which were widespread among ___E:Congregational U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregationalism_in_the_United_States)___ ministers and which placed these ministers and their congregations at odds with more traditionalist, ___E:Calvinist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformed_Christianity)___ pastors and clergies.  : 1–4 Following the death of ___E:Hollis Professor of Divinity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollis_Professor_of_Divinity)___ ___E:David Tappan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Tappan)___ in 1803 and that of ___E:Joseph Willard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Willard)___ , Harvard's eleventh president, the following year, a struggle broke out over their replacements.
In 1805, ___E:Henry Ware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ware_(Unitarian))___ was elected to replace Tappan as Hollis chair.

Two years later, in 1807, liberal ___E:Samuel Webber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Webber)___ was appointed as Harvard's 13th president, representing a shift from traditional ideas at Harvard to more liberal and ___E:Arminian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arminianism)___ ideas.  : 4–5  : 24

In 1816, Harvard University launched new language programs in the study of ___E:French U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language)___ and ___E:Spanish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language)___ , and appointed ___E:George Ticknor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Ticknor)___ the university's first professor for these language programs.

From 1869 to 1909, ___E:Charles William Eliot U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_William_Eliot)___ , Harvard University's 21st president, decreased the historically favored position of ___E:Christianity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity)___ in the curriculum, opening it to student self-direction.

Though Eliot was an influential figure in the secularization of U.S. higher education, he was motivated primarily by ___E:Transcendentalist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transcendentalism)___ and ___E:Unitarian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitarianism)___ convictions influenced by ___E:William Ellery Channing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ellery_Channing)___ , ___E:Ralph Waldo Emerson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ralph_Waldo_Emerson)___ , and others, rather than secularism.
In the late 19th century, Harvard University's graduate schools began admitting women in small numbers.
In 1900, Harvard became a founding member of the ___E:Association of American Universities U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_American_Universities)___ .

For the first few decades of the 20th century, the Harvard student body was predominantly "old-stock, high-status ___E:Protestants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protestantism)___ , especially ___E:Episcopalians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States))___ , ___E:Congregationalists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_church)___ , and ___E:Presbyterians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presbyterianism)___ ," according to sociologist and author ___E:Jerome Karabel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Karabel)___ .

Over the 20th century, as its endowment burgeoned and prominent intellectuals and professors affiliated with it, Harvard University's reputation as one of the world's most prestigious universities grew notably.

The university's enrollment also underwent substantial growth, a product of both the founding of new graduate academic programs and an expansion of the ___E:undergraduate college U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_College)___ . ___E:Radcliffe College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radcliffe_College)___ emerged as the female counterpart of Harvard College, becoming one of the most prominent schools in the nation for women.

In 1923, a year after the proportion of ___E:Jewish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews)___ students at Harvard reached 20%, ___E:A. Lawrence Lowell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A._Lawrence_Lowell)___ , the university's 22nd president, unsuccessfully proposed capping the admission of Jewish students to 15% of the undergraduate population.

Lowell also refused to mandate forced desegregation in the university's ___E:freshman dormitories U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Harvard_College_freshman_dormitories)___ , writing that, "We owe to the colored man the same opportunities for education that we do to the white man, but we do not owe to him to force him and the white into social relations that are not, or may not be, mutually congenial."

Between 1933 and 1953, Harvard University was led by ___E:James B. Conant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_B._Conant)___ , the university's 23rd president, who reinvigorated the university's creative scholarship in an effort to guarantee Harvard's preeminence among the nation and world's emerging research institutions.
Conant viewed higher education as a vehicle of opportunity for the talented rather than an entitlement for the wealthy, and devised programs to identify, recruit, and support talented youth.

In 1945, under Conant's leadership, an influential 268-page report, General Education in a Free Society , was published by Harvard faculty, which remains one of the most important works in ___E:curriculum studies U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curriculum_studies)___ ,  and women were first admitted to the ___E:medical school U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Medical_School)___ .
Between 1945 and 1960, admissions were standardized to open the university to a more diverse group of students.
Following the end of ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , for example, special exams were developed so veterans could be considered for admission.

No longer drawing mostly from prestigious ___E:prep schools U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College-preparatory_school)___ in ___E:New England U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_England)___ , the undergraduate college became accessible to striving middle class students from public schools; many more Jews and Catholics were admitted, but Blacks, Hispanics, and Asians remained underrepresented.
Over the second half of the 20th century, however, the university became incrementally more diverse.
Between 1971 and 1999, Harvard controlled undergraduate admission, instruction, and housing for Radcliffe's women; in 1999, Radcliffe was formally merged into Harvard University.

On July 1, 2007, ___E:Drew Gilpin Faust U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drew_Gilpin_Faust)___ , dean of ___E:Harvard Radcliffe Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Radcliffe_Institute)___ , was appointed Harvard's 28th and the university's first female president.

On July 1, 2018, Faust retired and joined the board of ___E:Goldman Sachs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs)___ , and ___E:Lawrence Bacow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Bacow)___ became Harvard's ___E:29th president U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_Harvard_University)___ .
In February 2023, approximately 6,000 Harvard workers attempted to organize a union.

Bacow retired in June 2023, and on July 1 ___E:Claudine Gay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudine_Gay)___ , a Harvard professor in the Government and African American Studies departments and Dean of the ___E:Faculty of Arts and Sciences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Faculty_of_Arts_and_Sciences)___ , became Harvard's 30th president.

In January 2024, just six months into her presidency, Gay resigned following ___E:allegations of antisemitism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudine_Gay#Congressional_hearing_on_antisemitism)___ and ___E:plagiarism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudine_Gay#Plagiarism_investigations)___ .
Gay was succeeded by ___E:Alan Garber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Garber)___ , the university's provost, who was appointed interim president.
In August 2024, the university announced that Garber would be appointed Harvard's 31st president through the end of the 2026–27 academic year.

In February 2025, ___E:Leo Terrell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Terrell)___ , the head of the Trump administration's ___E:Task Force to Combat Antisemitism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism_in_the_United_States#Efforts_to_combat_antisemitism)___ , announced that he would investigate Harvard University as part of the Department of Justice's broader investigation into ___E:antisemitism on college campuses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism_in_US_higher_education)___ .

In April 2025, the United States federal government under President ___E:Donald Trump U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump)___ threatened to withhold nearly $9 billion in government funds from the university unless the university complied with government demands to modify many of its policies.

This threat was part of a broader battle over universities' autonomy following contentious ___E:student protests U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_pro-Palestinian_protests_on_university_campuses)___ against the ___E:Gaza war U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaza_war)___ , and followed ___E:similar demands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_policy_of_the_second_Donald_Trump_administration#Actions_against_universities)___ made of ___E:Columbia University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University)___ .
The university's leadership resisted the government's demands, claiming that they were an unlawful overreach of government authority.
In response, the ___E:US Department of Education U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Department_of_Education)___ announced they were freezing $2.3 billion in federal funds to Harvard.

The ___E:Department of Homeland Security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Homeland_Security)___ subsequently threatened to revoke Harvard's eligibility to host ___E:international students U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_student)___ .

Harvard responded by filing ___E:a lawsuit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_and_Fellows_of_Harvard_College_v._Department_of_Health_and_Human_Services)___ against the Trump administration in the ___E:District Court of Massachusetts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_District_Court_for_the_District_of_Massachusetts)___ , arguing that the freezing of funds was unconstitutional.

In May 2025, education secretary ___E:Linda McMahon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_McMahon)___ informed Harvard president Garber that the federal government would no longer provide grant funding until the university complied with the Trump administration's demands.
The following week, the Trump administration cut an additional $450 million in grants to the school.

Later that same month, Department of Homeland Security secretary ___E:Kristi Noem U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristi_Noem)___ announced that Harvard's ___E:Student and Exchange Visitor Program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student_and_Exchange_Visitor_Program)___ certification had been revoked, barring Harvard from hosting international students.
The following day, Harvard sued the Trump administration for banning them from enrolling international students and U.S.

District Judge ___E:Allison Burroughs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allison_D._Burroughs)___ granted a temporary restraining order stopping the ban.     On June 16, 2025, Burroughs postponed a ruling after hearing arguments from lawyers on both sides, leaving the temporary block in place for another week.

On May 30, 2025, the ___E:State Department U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State)___ ordered all US embassies and consulates to conduct "comprehensive and thorough vetting" of the online presence of anyone seeking to visit Harvard from abroad.

On June 4, 2025, Trump issued a proclamation restricting international students from studying at Harvard, and directing the State Department to consider revoking the visas of current international students studying at that university.
The following day, Harvard filed a legal challenge, amending their existing federal complaint against the administration.
On June 20, Harvard was granted an injunction allowing it to continue hosting international students as litigation continues.
On June 30, a Trump administration investigation found Harvard violated federal civil rights law by failing to protect Jewish students, faculty, and staff.

On September 3, 2025 US District Judge ___E:Allison Burroughs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allison_D._Burroughs)___ ruled the Trump administration illegally froze more than $2 billion in research funding stating the administration "...violated Harvard's free-speech rights as well as the US Civil Rights Act."

The 209-acre (85 ha) main campus of Harvard University is centered on ___E:Harvard Yard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Yard)___ , colloquially known as "the Yard", in ___E:Cambridge, Massachusetts U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts)___ , about three miles (five km) west-northwest of downtown ___E:Boston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)___ , and extending to the surrounding ___E:Harvard Square U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Square)___ neighborhood.

The Yard houses several Harvard buildings, including four of the university's libraries, ___E:Houghton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houghton_Library)___ , ___E:Lamont U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamont_Library)___ , ___E:Pusey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pusey_Library)___ , and ___E:Widener U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widener_Library)___ .

Also on Harvard Yard are ___E:Massachusetts Hall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Hall_(Harvard_University))___ , built between 1718 and 1720 and the university's oldest still standing building, ___E:Memorial Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Church_of_Harvard_University)___ , and ___E:University Hall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Hall_(Harvard_University))___ .

Harvard Yard and adjacent areas include the main academic buildings of the ___E:Faculty of Arts and Sciences U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Faculty_of_Arts_and_Sciences)___ , including ___E:Sever Hall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sever_Hall)___ , ___E:Harvard Hall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Hall)___ , and ___E:freshman dormitories U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Harvard_College_freshman_dormitories)___ .

Upperclassmen live in the twelve ___E:residential houses U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_House_system)___ , located south of Harvard Yard near the ___E:Charles River U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_River)___ and on ___E:Radcliffe Quadrangle U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radcliffe_Quadrangle_(Harvard))___ , which formerly housed ___E:Radcliffe College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radcliffe_College)___ students.
Each house is a community of undergraduates, faculty deans, and resident tutors, with its own dining hall, library, and recreational facilities.

Also on the main campus in Cambridge are the ___E:Law U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Law_School)___ , ___E:Divinity U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Divinity_School)___ (theology), ___E:Engineering and Applied Science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_John_A._Paulson_School_of_Engineering_and_Applied_Sciences)___ , ___E:Design U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Graduate_School_of_Design)___ (architecture), ___E:Education U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Graduate_School_of_Education)___ , ___E:Kennedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Kennedy_School)___ (public policy), and ___E:Extension U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Extension_School)___ schools, and ___E:Harvard Radcliffe Institute U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Radcliffe_Institute)___ in Radcliffe Yard.  Harvard also has commercial real estate holdings in Cambridge.

___E:Harvard Business School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Business_School)___ , ___E:Harvard Innovation Labs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Innovation_Labs)___ , and many athletics facilities, including ___E:Harvard Stadium U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Stadium)___ , are located on a 358-acre (145 ha) campus in the ___E:Allston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allston)___ section of ___E:Boston U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston)___ across the ___E:John W.
